questions.q: Using $I(p) = -\log_2(p)$, how many bits of surprise does an event with probability $p = 1/8$ carry?
questions.explain: $-\log_2(1/8) = \log_2 8 = 3$ bits: like three fair coin flips. The minus sign makes surprise non-negative, so $-3$ is impossible.

questions.q: You flip a fair coin and roll a fair die (independent). What is the total surprise of seeing a specific coin face *and* a specific die face?
questions.explain: Probabilities multiply ($\frac{1}{2}\cdot\frac{1}{6} = \frac{1}{12}$) and the log turns that into a sum: $1 + 2.585 = 3.585$ bits. That additivity is exactly why surprise uses a logarithm.

questions.q: A framework reports a cross-entropy loss of $-\ln(0.01) \approx 4.61$ for one example. What is this surprise in **bits**?
questions.explain: Frameworks use the natural log, so $4.61$ is in nats. $1$ nat $= 1/\ln 2 \approx 1.443$ bits, so $4.61 \times 1.443 \approx 6.64$ bits $= -\log_2(0.01)$. $3.19$ divides instead of multiplying; $2.00$ is $-\log_{10}(0.01)$.

questions.q: A classifier gives the true class probability 0.99 in one case and 0.01 in another. Which statement matches the page?
options: The 0.01 case gives a huge surprise (≈ 6.64 bits) and a large loss; the 0.99 case is almost zero
Both cases give the same loss because the probabilities sum to 1
The 0.99 case gives the larger loss because the model is overconfident
Surprise only depends on whether the prediction is right, not on the probability
questions.explain: $-\log_2(0.99) \approx 0.014$ bits vs. $-\log_2(0.01) \approx 6.64$ bits. For a one-hot label, this surprise *is* the cross-entropy loss, so being confidently wrong is punished heavily.
